### Diagnosing Hot Soak Start Failures on Direct Injection V8s

The symptom you are describingâstarting fine cold, but requiring excessive cranking after the car has sat for a couple of hoursâis a classic "hot soak" failure mode. On an Audi S5 V8 FSI with direct injection (DI), this behavior almost exclusively points to fuel system integrity rather than a temperature sensor fault. While the Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) sensor data might appear sluggish or show delayed ramp-up rates, that is frequently secondary behavior caused by the engine management system detecting a lean condition during the hot soak period.

The core issue here is likely residual fuel dripping into the intake runners or cylinders while the engine is off, followed by vaporization upon restart. Direct injection engines are particularly sensitive to this because there is no throttle body bowl to catch overflow; fuel sprays directly onto the piston crown. If injectors are leaking internally or if the high-pressure pump seals are degrading under heat, fuel accumulates in the intake tract during the "off" period.

When you turn the key after sitting for two hours, that pooled liquid fuel begins to vaporize instantly due to the hot metal surfaces of the combustion chamber and intake manifold. This creates an extremely rich air-fuel mixture in the cylinders. The ECU attempts to start the engine, but the spark plugs are firing into a cloud of unburned vapor rather than a stable mixture. You will hear the cranking sound persist longer because the mixture is too rich to ignite immediately; once the excess fuel burns off or the throttle position changes enough to draw air through the system, combustion resumes, which explains why the car eventually lurches to life.

The smell of petrol you detect near one of the cylinders confirms that liquid fuel is entering the intake port. The fact that the plug is dry on top but wet inside the cylinder suggests the fuel is bypassing the valve and pooling in the combustion chamber or sitting in the valley between the intake runners, waiting for heat to turn it into vapor.

Your observation regarding the ECT sensor readings warrants a closer look, specifically at the "slow" response time. On many Bosch-Med4/Motronic systems common in VW/Audi V8s, if the ECU detects that the engine is running on a significantly richer mixture than expected (due to injector leaks), it may not aggressively command enrichment corrections because the lambda sensor isn't providing a valid feedback loop during cranking. This can make the coolant temperature reading appear sluggish as the system tries to compensate for the perceived load, even if the physical sensor is fine. However, replacing the ECT sensor without addressing the fuel leak is a temporary fix that will likely return the same symptoms once the new sensor warms up and the rich condition persists.

The manual carbon cleaning you performed introduced a variable: debris left in the injector support area. While unlikely to cause a mechanical leak on its own, any foreign material trapped near the injector O-rings or within the valve guide seals can exacerbate seal degradation over time, especially under the high thermal cycling of a V8 engine. The Liqui Moly cleaner may have also loosened deposits that were acting as minor seals around older injectors, temporarily improving flow but potentially leaving gaps exposed to heat.

Before replacing the ECT sensor, verify the fuel rail pressure decay test with the ignition on and engine off. If the pressure drops from 25 bar to near zero within a few minutes while the key is in the "on" position (but not cranking), you have a confirmed injector seal failure or a faulty high-pressure pump accumulator. The fact that your rail pressure remains stable after two hours suggests the leak might be intermittent or dependent on the specific thermal expansion of the engine block, which often happens with aging rubber O-rings in the intake manifold rails common to the V8 FSI architecture.

Check the injector electrical connectors for corrosion or moisture ingress, as a poor ground can sometimes mimic a leakage fault by causing erratic injector pulse widths. If the pressure holds but the smell persists, inspect the valve guide seals; they may be worn and allowing fuel to drip past the intake valves into the cylinder during shutdown. Addressing the root cause of the fuel leak will restore normal starting behavior far more reliably than swapping sensors.
